title: What Krishna told Arjuna first
hookLine: a warrior drops his bow, and Krishna's first teaching hides a second 'not' inside one word
carry: atman: the real in you never stops being
tomorrow: one hidden a, and two schools read a line opposite ways?

cards: Two armies face each other on the field of Kurukshetra, and the best archer on either side sits down in his chariot. Arjuna has looked across and seen his teachers, his cousins, old Bhishma who helped raise him.
His bow slips from his hand. I will not fight, he says, and goes quiet. His charioteer is Krishna.

In the Gita's telling, Krishna smiles, and begins not with tactics but with this: you grieve for what should not be grieved. Then a line Hindus have loved ever since: nasato vidyate bhavo, nabhavo vidyate satah.

teach.h: THE UNREAL NEVER COMES TO BE.
teach.b: Roughly: the unreal never comes to be; the real never stops being. And there's a small puzzle in it worth solving, because it holds the whole teaching. Each half seems to have one not: na.

But there are two. Sanskrit turns a word into its opposite with a short a in front: sat, the real; asat, the unreal. When na meets asat, the two a's melt into one long a, and the second not slips out of sight.
Na, asatah: nasato. So what is the real that never stops being? Krishna says it in the verses around this one: the Self, the atman, the one who lives in the body.
Bodies are born, change and end, the way clothes are worn and set aside.

The atman isn't born and doesn't die. Weapons don't cut it; fire doesn't burn it. That's the Gita's first teaching, and it's one reason many Hindu families read the Gita, often chapter two, when someone dies.
It doesn't say the loss isn't real. Arjuna's tears are real, and Krishna doesn't mock them. It says the person you love was never only the body you're losing.
And once Arjuna has heard it, Krishna turns him back toward what he has to do. In the Gita, grief isn't the end of the road. It's where the teaching starts.

how: Many Hindu families read from the Bhagavad Gita at a death or a memorial, often from chapter two; students reading it in Sanskrit split joined words like nasato with a word-by-word gloss.

o: undoing joins to find the words inside
a rule for which vowels are held long
a way of reading a verse faster aloud

games.q: at a friend's grandfather's memorial, the family reads from the Gita, chapter two. your friend whispers: 'why this part?' what do you say?
o: it's Krishna's first teaching: the atman isn't born and doesn't die; only the body ends.
it's a battle chapter, read to honor how brave he was.
it says grief is wrong, so nobody should cry today.
games.why: chapter two is where Krishna tells a grieving Arjuna that the real self doesn't end. it comforts without pretending the loss isn't real.

practice: If you keep a Gita at home, open it to chapter two and read verse sixteen slowly, once. If not, just hold its meaning: the unreal never comes to be; the real never stops being.
Then bring to mind one person or thing you're afraid to lose. Don't push the fear away. Set beside it the question Krishna sets beside Arjuna's tears: what here is real, and can't be taken?

wordCard.voice: Sandhi plainly: where words meet and melt. Today, two short a's melting into one long one, and a second not hiding inside nasato.

orig.note: Sanskrit: of the unreal there is no being (Bhagavad Gita 2.16).

carryVoice: For the road: atman, the real in you never stops being. Bodies change like clothes; the Self doesn't. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: nasato vidyate bhavo, nabhavo vidyate satah

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.16 (meaning: of the unreal no being, of the real no non-being)
Bhagavad Gita 1.47 and 2.9–2.11 (Arjuna sets down his bow; Krishna, smiling, says he grieves for what should not be grieved)
Bhagavad Gita 2.20–2.23 (the Self is not born and does not die; bodies set aside like worn clothes; weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it)
Ashtadhyayi 6.1.101 (akah savarne dirghah: like vowels join as one long vowel)
